title: Good Time Charlie by Ryan J. Haddad at The Public Theater #goodtimech...
transcript: Every theatre kid has a gateway show or a relative that they can thank for their obsession, and for Ryan J. Haddad, it's his uncle Charlie. In this tender new play, Ryan honors Charlie, who channeled his passion for theatre into Ryan after abandoning his dreams for dentistry. Ryan sets the scene through a direct opening address and then frequently narrates throughout a series of generally chronological events from his and Charlie's lives. Like Ryan, all the other characters are framed in a way as if they're playing themselves, together telling this story because Ryan has asked them to. It makes the piece more meta and allows us a look into the questions Ryan is grappling with as a playwright. Being open and confessional seems like second nature to him, but in this piece, he has to consider where that line is when it comes to other people who are real and who he deeply cares about. While certainly interesting, the framing device feels pretty clunky in the first half hour or so. The transitions feel jerky and the characters are hastily introduced, appearing in quick succession with an air of cheesy pageantry. As the piece progresses, however, the tone becomes more endearing as we see Charlie stoically support his life partner, his family, and Ryan through hard times, leaning on humor and the arts as a vital source of comfort. Although there are plenty of funny moments in the show, the serious ones shine the brightest, movingly tying together and contrasting the experiences Charlie and Ryan have both had, not just as theatre enthusiasts but also as gay men. All that said, it's hard not to compare this piece to the stunningly specific solo work Ryan has previously created about his experiences being gay and disabled. The focus on theatre, found family, and queer mentors is definitely a road that's been more travelled, but Ryan's reflective and fearless approach makes this one distinctly his.
